headings.text: A plugin is a separate APK
The one rule that trips everyone up: two Contexts

blocks.html:
Before writing any code, it helps to understand what an ATAK plugin actually is and how ATAK finds and runs it. The model is small — once it clicks, the rest of the guide is just detail.

A plugin is a separate APK

An ATAK plugin is its own Android application (APK), built and signed separately from ATAK, and installed alongside it on the device. It is not compiled into ATAK. At runtime ATAK discovers installed plugin APKs, loads their code into its own process, and calls into them.

Because the plugin runs inside ATAK's process, it gets direct access to ATAK's APIs — the map, CoT messaging, overlays, preferences, and so on. The trade-off is that this internal API can change between ATAK versions, so a plugin is built against a specific ATAK API version (more on that in Build, install & run).

How ATAK discovers a plugin

Two things make an installed APK visible to ATAK as a plugin:

  1. A discovery entry in **AndroidManifest.xml**. The plugin declares an activity for the well-known action com.atakmap.app.component, which is how ATAK enumerates installed plugins:

    <!-- allow for plugin discovery -->
<activity android:name="com.atakmap.app.component"
    tools:ignore="MissingClass">
    <intent-filter android:label="@string/app_name">
        <action android:name="com.atakmap.app.component" />
    </intent-filter>
</activity>

  2. An API-version marker, also in the manifest, that tells ATAK which API this plugin was built for:

    <meta-data android:name="plugin-api" android:value="${atakApiVersion}"/>

    ${atakApiVersion} is filled in at build time by the Gradle product flavor you build (e.g. com.atakmap.app@5.6.0.CIV). ATAK refuses to load a plugin whose API marker doesn't match the running app — this is the compatibility gate.

The four building blocks

Every plugin is assembled from the same handful of classes. The official helloworld example defines exactly four small "plumbing" classes; everything else is your own feature code.

Block Base class Role
Plugin (Lifecycle) AbstractPlugin (implements gov.tak.api.plugin.IPlugin) Entry point. ATAK's service controller constructs it; it wires in your Tool and MapComponent(s).
MapComponent DropDownMapComponent The unit of functionality. Registers receivers, hooks map/CoT events, cleans up.
Tool AbstractPluginTool The toolbar/nav button the user taps to open your plugin.
DropDown receiver DropDownReceiver Your UI panel that slides in, plus the actions that drive it.

These are bound to ATAK through a small **assets/plugin.xml** file. In ATAK 5.x it declares a single extension — your plugin entry point, of type gov.tak.api.plugin.IPlugin:

<plugin>
    <extension
        type="gov.tak.api.plugin.IPlugin"
        impl="com.atakmap.android.helloworld.plugin.HelloWorldLifecycle"
        singleton="true" />
</plugin>

That one class (an AbstractPlugin) constructs and registers your Tool (the button) and your MapComponent(s) in code — so unlike older ATAK, the Tool is not declared separately in plugin.xml. We build it in The plugin lifecycle and the UI in Build a UI.

Changed in ATAK 5.x. ATAK 4.x used the transapps framework and declared two plugin.xml extensions — a transapps.maps.plugin.lifecycle.Lifecycle and a transapps.maps.plugin.tool.ToolDescriptor. ATAK 5.x replaces both with the single gov.tak.api.plugin.IPlugin entry point shown above. If you're reading an older tutorial or a 4.x plugin, that's the key difference to translate.

The one rule that trips everyone up: two Contexts

A plugin lives in two worlds at once, so two different **android.content.Context** objects are in play, and they are not interchangeable:

  • The plugin context resolves resources (layouts, drawables, strings) from your plugin's APK.
  • The MapView context is ATAK's own UI context, used for anything that touches the screen — AlertDialog, Toast, etc.

⚠️ Using the plugin context to construct an **AlertDialog** will throw a runtime error. Inflate your layouts and load your resources with the plugin context; show dialogs and toasts with the MapView context (getMapView().getContext()).

Keep this distinction in mind from the start — it is the single most common source of crashes in new plugins, and it's called out explicitly in the example plugin's own README.
